samples.text:
In many countries, the number of young voters in elections is lower than older voters. This essay will explain some reasons for this and the consequences it has for society.

There are several reasons why young people do not vote. Firstly, many young people are not interested in politics because they think it is boring and complicated. They do not understand the difference between the parties, so they do not know who to choose. Secondly, a lot of young people believe that their vote cannot change anything. They see that politicians make promises before elections but they do not keep them after, so they lose trust. Also, some young people are students who live far from their hometown, and it is not easy for them to register or go to the polling station on election day.

This situation has some serious consequences. The most important one is that politicians focus more on older people, because older people vote more. For example, government may spend more money on pensions and less on education or cheap housing for young families. As a result, young people problems are ignored and they feel even less connected to politics. Another consequence is that the democracy becomes weaker, because the government does not represent the whole population. In the future, if this young people never start voting, the problem will become more serious.

In conclusion, young people vote less because they are not interested, they do not trust politicians and voting is not convenient for them. This leads to policies which favour older people and a weaker democracy. I think schools should teach more about politics to encourage young people to vote.
samples.why: Both questions answered with relevant reasons and consequences · development is limited and repetitive (young people, older people) · mechanical linking · errors in comparison, articles and possessives that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
Election results in many countries show that turnout among younger citizens is considerably lower than among older age groups. This essay will explore the reasons for this pattern and discuss its consequences for society as a whole.

One of the main reasons is a sense of disconnection from mainstream politics. Many young people feel that political parties are dominated by older politicians who neither understand nor prioritise their concerns, such as housing costs, job insecurity and climate change. As a result, they conclude that voting will make little difference. Another factor is a lack of political education. Unless they grow up in families that discuss current affairs, young adults may find the system confusing and feel unqualified to make a choice. Practical obstacles also play a role; students and young workers move house frequently, and if registration rules are complicated, they may simply not be registered in the right place when an election is called.

The consequences of low youth turnout are significant. Since politicians naturally pay attention to those who vote, policies tend to favour older voters, for example through generous pension increases, while issues affecting young people receive less attention and funding. This creates a vicious cycle, because young people then feel even more excluded from the political process and become less likely to participate in future. In the long term, this undermines the legitimacy of democratic institutions, as governments are elected by an increasingly unrepresentative section of the population. It may also encourage some young people to express their frustration through protest rather than through the ballot box.

In conclusion, young people vote less because they feel ignored, lack political knowledge and faces practical barriers. The result is a political system that neglects their interests, which in turn weakens democracy.
samples.why: Both parts answered clearly with extended causes and consequences · logical progression (vicious cycle) · good range of vocabulary (turnout, legitimacy, unrepresentative) · mostly error-free sentences with one agreement slip.

samples.text:
In many democracies, a striking generational divide exists at the ballot box, with people in their late teens and twenties voting at markedly lower rates than their parents and grandparents. This gap can be traced to disillusionment, limited political education and practical barriers, and its consequences extend well beyond young people themselves.

Perhaps the most significant factor is a perception that politics is not designed for them. Young voters frequently see parliaments dominated by older figures and debates that seem remote from their immediate concerns, such as unaffordable rents or insecure employment. When the connection between casting a vote and improving one's own life appears weak, abstaining can seem a rational response rather than mere apathy. This detachment is reinforced by inadequate civic education; many school leavers have little understanding of how government works or how party programmes differ, and uncertainty easily turns into disengagement. Practical obstacles add a further layer. Young adults change address frequently for study or work, and cumbersome registration procedures can mean that they are unable to vote even if they wish to.

The consequences for society are considerable. Politicians seeking re-election rationally direct their attention towards the groups most likely to turn out, which can result in policies that protect pensions and property values while underinvesting in education, affordable housing and long-term environmental measures. Such imbalances can deepen intergenerational inequality and, in turn, reinforce young people's belief that the system ignores them, creating a self-perpetuating cycle. More broadly, a government chosen by a narrowing slice of the electorate risks losing legitimacy, and frustration that finds no outlet at the ballot box may emerge instead as distrust or unrest.

In conclusion, low youth turnout stems from disillusionment, limited civic knowledge and practical hurdles. Its effects, from skewed policy priorities to weakened democratic legitimacy, make it a problem for the whole of society rather than for young people alone.
samples.why: Both questions fully answered with sophisticated, well-linked analysis · ideas extended and logically sequenced · precise, wide-ranging vocabulary (abstaining, cumbersome, self-perpetuating) · complex structures used accurately throughout.
